preamble: A direct shift of the voiceless dental fricative [θ] to the voiceless velar fricative [x] is very rare. The one well-documented case is in North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic: in the Christian dialect of Gerbish, where *θ is normally debuccalized to /h/, it surfaces as /x/ next to emphatic (pharyngealized) /ṛ/. Khan (2023) explains it by the pharyngeal constriction of /ṛ/ narrowing the airflow, which gives [x] rather than [h]. He also suggests the change may have gone through an emphatic sibilant (*θ > *ṣ > x).

examples.note: Only next to emphatic /ṛ/; elsewhere *θ becomes /h/ in this dialect (bɛha < *bayθa 'house').
Khan cites one parallel in Jewish Barzani: nxaṛa < *nθara 'to fall off (leaves)'.
Khan suggests an intermediate emphatic sibilant (*θ > *ṣ > x), since *θ gives /ṣ/ in other emphatic words of the same dialect (ʾaṣṛa < *ʾaθra 'country').

sources: Khan, G. (2023). Interdental consonants in North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic dialects. Kervan 27(2). https://doi.org/10.13135/1825-263X/8225
